title: Retell a finding in your own words
objective: Keep the meaning when you paraphrase. Keep the main idea when you summarize.

slides.title: Choose what your reader needs
body: A paraphrase restates the same idea in your own words. Keep important details.
A summary is shorter. Choose the ideas that answer your question. Credit the source in both.

slides.title: Read, cover, retell and check
body: Class note by Dao: “The class counted three frogs at dusk.”
Paraphrase: Dao reports that students saw three frogs when the day was ending.
Check who, what, how many and when. Keep scientific terms if another word would change the meaning.

slides.title: Read the first case together
body: Classroom source: Field Note A, by Mali. “Students saw twelve butterflies in the sunny garden. They saw five in the shaded garden. They watched each garden for ten minutes.”

slides.title: Try it with a partner
body: Retell the two counts in your own words. Name the source.
Write a one-sentence summary of the main finding.
Change the order of the places.

slides.title: Try a new case
body: Classroom source: Field Note B, by Niran. “Students saw nine birds beside the pond. They saw four in the field. They watched each place for ten minutes.”

slides.title: Work on your own
body: Retell the two counts in your own words. Name the source.
Write a one-sentence summary of the main finding.
Name one detail your summary kept and one it left out. Explain your choice.

slides.title: Compare your two versions
body: Underline a detail in your paraphrase. Does your shorter summary still answer the main question?
